about.p: Reefresh, Maybe Next Time is a participatory art and education project about the future of coral reefs. It starts from a speculative future in which corals as we know them no longer exist. The corals gathered here have gone on evolving over many generations: new colours, shapes, organs, defences and behaviours, so that they might survive conditions that have changed around them.

The project brings together climate protection, science, design and collective storytelling. It draws attention to what coral reefs mean and to the threat climate change poses to them — and it shows that the future is not only something to be predicted, but something that can be imagined and shaped together.

about.lead: What would a coral have to become in order to go on living in a sea altered by climate change and by us?

about.p: Working from one shared coral template, participants designed their own corals of the future. They decided how their coral had changed, what particular abilities it had gained, and why those adaptations had become necessary for its survival. The result: corals with armour, new organs, technical extensions, symbioses with other creatures, and survival strategies entirely their own.

To make it happen I approached a great many institutions, presented the idea and got into conversation with all kinds of people. Some places I visited myself, to explain the project on site and to keep the participants company while they drew.

Stations were set up in several places. The template, drawing materials and information about the project lay ready, and anyone who wanted to could design their own coral and add their own idea of how a living thing might answer the consequences of climate change.

about.p: Collecting the drawings was where the second, larger part of the work began. Every design was reviewed, ordered and prepared digitally: the hand-drawn corals were reconstructed as clean two-dimensional drawings and then translated into naturalistic three-dimensional ones.

The original ideas, the handwritten notes and the particular features each participant had given their coral were carried carefully across. Every coral was given characteristics of its own and an invented evolutionary history explaining why it looks or behaves as it does. Alongside them came scientific-looking detail studies in the manner of historical biological archives.

The three-dimensional corals were generated from the prepared drawings with an AI image-to-3D process (Tripo) and reworked by hand afterwards. Every environment, variety name and evolutionary history is invented and has been editorially reviewed. No specimen depicts a coral that exists.

Reefresh, Maybe Next Time does not claim that corals can simply adapt to what climate change does to them. The fantastical changes show the opposite: how extraordinary, and in places how drastic, that development would have to be for them to go on living under conditions that keep getting harder.

The project invites people to think about the consequences of human action, makes the importance of healthy reefs visible, and strengthens the sense that the future can be shaped. Participants are not only confronted with a possible future — they develop ideas for it themselves. Out of many drawings, stories and points of view comes one shared account of adaptation, responsibility, and the question of which future we want to build for the world around us.
Every specimen goes back to the same template: Desmophyllum pertusum, a cold-water stony coral that builds reefs in cold, dark water far below 1000 metres.

Each one has been given an invented setting here: the sea it would have needed for exactly this adaptation to make sense. The years arrange those scenarios into one possible sequence — they are narrative, not forecast.
The variety names are invented too. Where the person who drew it is known, the coral carries their name; otherwise the name describes its most striking adaptation.

Together, we travel into the future — down into the dark deep sea. Climate change has altered that habitat too, and many deep-sea corals are struggling under the new conditions. But then a new species is discovered: it has developed a particular defence that helps it cope with the consequences.

about.lead: Draw your deep-sea coral of the future, and show what protection it has developed.

about.p: Biologically accurate, freely invented, unusual or completely mad — anything goes. There are no right or wrong answers.

step: 1. Take a sheet of paper and a pencil.
Draw how a coral might protect itself from the consequences of climate change.
Whether you write your name on the sheet is up to you. If you do, it becomes the scientific name of the coral you invented.
4. Drop the finished sheet into the box.
